topics.summary: Indices, surds and logarithms are three views of the same idea: powers, roots and the exponents that undo them. They underpin almost every algebra round in NSMQ, where questions ask you to simplify an expression or solve an exponential equation in seconds.
keyIdeas: A logarithm is an exponent: logₐx = y means aʸ = x, with a > 0, a ≠ 1 and x > 0.
a⁰ = 1 for any a ≠ 0, and a negative index means a reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
A fractional index a^(m/n) means the nth root raised to the power m.
A surd is an irrational root such as √2; simplify by taking out square factors: √72 = √36 × √2 = 6√2.
Rationalise a denominator by multiplying by its conjugate: (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b.
To solve an exponential equation, write both sides with the same base or take logs of both sides.
log means base 10 and ln means base e unless a base is written.

formulas.name: Product and quotient of powers
formulas.formula: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ ;  aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
formulas.note: Same base only; add or subtract the indices.

formulas.name: Power of a power
formulas.note: Multiply indices; the power spreads over a product, not a sum.

formulas.name: Fractional index
formulas.note: Take the root first to keep numbers small: 32^(3/5) = 2³ = 8.

formulas.name: Rationalising a binomial surd
formulas.note: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

formulas.name: Nested square root
formulas.formula: √(a + 2√b) = √x + √y, where x + y = a and xy = b
formulas.note: Find two numbers with sum a and product b; for a − 2√b use √x − √y with x > y.

formulas.name: Laws of logarithms
formulas.formula: logₐ(xy) = logₐx + logₐy ;  logₐ(x/y) = logₐx − logₐy ;  logₐ(xⁿ) = n logₐx
formulas.note: Valid for x, y > 0.

formulas.name: Special values
formulas.note: A power and a log of the same base cancel.

formulas.name: Change of base
formulas.note: m is any convenient base, usually 10 or e.

formulas.name: Reciprocal rule
formulas.note: Follows from change of base; useful when bases and arguments swap.

formulas.name: Number of digits
formulas.formula: Number of digits of N = ⌊log N⌋ + 1
formulas.note: For a positive integer N, using base-10 log.

shortcuts.name: Telescoping log chain
shortcuts.rule: In logₐm × logₘn × logₙp each argument cancels the next base, leaving logₐp.
shortcuts.example: log₂3 × log₃4 × log₄8 = log₂8 = 3.

shortcuts.name: Know your power tables
shortcuts.rule: Memorise powers of 2 to 2¹⁰ = 1024, of 3 to 3⁶ = 729 and of 5 to 5⁵ = 3125, then rewrite every number as a prime power.

shortcuts.name: Nested surd by sum–product
shortcuts.rule: Write the inner surd as 2√b, then find two numbers adding to a and multiplying to b.
shortcuts.example: √(7 + 4√3) = √(7 + 2√12): numbers with sum 7 and product 12 are 4 and 3, so the answer is 2 + √3. Check: (2 + √3)² = 7 + 4√3.

shortcuts.name: log 2 and log 3 anchors
shortcuts.rule: Remember log 2 ≈ 0.3010 and log 3 ≈ 0.4771; build other logs from them (log 5 = 1 − log 2).

shortcuts.name: Conjugate product on sight
shortcuts.rule: (√a + √b)(√a − √b) is just a − b; never expand term by term.

traps: Writing log(a + b) = log a + log b; the product rule works only for log(ab).
Writing √(a + b) = √a + √b; √(9 + 16) = 5, not 7.
Confusing −3² = −9 with (−3)² = 9 when a negative base is not in brackets.
Forgetting to check answers of log equations: any solution that makes a log argument zero or negative must be rejected.
Adding indices of different bases: 2³ × 3² is not 6⁵.
nsmqTips: Questions often say 'simplify without a calculator'; convert every number to a prime power first.
For 'solve 2ˣ = 7' questions where no exact answer exists, give x = log 7 / log 2 and a decimal only if asked.
Say the final surd in simplest form with a rational denominator; quizmasters may not accept 1/√2 when √2/2 is expected.

topics.summary: A polynomial is a sum of whole-number powers of x with constant coefficients. The remainder and factor theorems let you find remainders and factors without long division, a classic fast NSMQ question.
keyIdeas: Division identity: f(x) = (divisor) × Q(x) + R(x), where the degree of R is less than the degree of the divisor.
Remainder theorem: dividing f(x) by (x − a) leaves remainder f(a).
Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor of f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0.
For a divisor (ax − b), substitute x = b/a.
Dividing by a quadratic leaves a remainder of the form px + q.
Sum and product of roots come straight from the coefficients, without solving.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots.

formulas.name: Remainder theorem
formulas.note: For (x + a) substitute x = −a.

formulas.name: Linear divisor ax − b
formulas.note: Set the divisor to zero and substitute.

formulas.name: Factor theorem
formulas.note: Used to test candidate roots and find unknown coefficients.

formulas.name: Quadratic roots
formulas.note: For ax² + bx + c = 0.

formulas.name: Cubic roots
formulas.formula: α + β + γ = −b/a ;  αβ + βγ + γα = c/a ;  αβγ = −d/a
formulas.note: For ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0.

formulas.name: Symmetric expressions
formulas.formula: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ ;  α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β)
formulas.note: Build any symmetric function from sum and product.

formulas.name: Difference of roots
formulas.note: Gives |α − β| = √(b² − 4ac)/|a|.

formulas.name: Sum and difference of cubes
formulas.formula: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) ;  a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
formulas.note: Standard factorisations.

formulas.name: Rational root test
formulas.formula: Any rational root p/q has p dividing the constant term and q dividing the leading coefficient
formulas.note: Narrows down which values to try.

shortcuts.name: Coefficient sum = f(1)
shortcuts.rule: If the coefficients add to zero, x = 1 is a root and (x − 1) is a factor.
shortcuts.example: 2x³ − 3x² − 5x + 6: 2 − 3 − 5 + 6 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor; the rest is 2x² − x − 6 = (2x + 3)(x − 2).

shortcuts.name: Alternating sum = f(−1)
shortcuts.rule: If the even-power coefficients add to the same as the odd-power coefficients, x = −1 is a root.
shortcuts.example: x³ + 2x² − x − 2: even powers 2 + (−2) = 0, odd powers 1 + (−1) = 0, so (x + 1) is a factor.

shortcuts.name: Synthetic division
shortcuts.rule: Write the coefficients, bring down the first, multiply by a and add along the row; the last number is the remainder.

shortcuts.name: Quadratic divisor by its roots
shortcuts.rule: To divide by (x − a)(x − b), write remainder px + q and substitute x = a and x = b.
shortcuts.example: x⁵ ÷ (x² − 1): p + q = 1 and −p + q = −1 give p = 1, q = 0, so the remainder is x.

shortcuts.name: Symmetric function without solving
shortcuts.rule: Get α + β and αβ from the coefficients, then use an identity.
shortcuts.example: Roots of x² − 5x + 3 = 0: α + β = 5, αβ = 3, so α² + β² = 25 − 6 = 19.

traps: Sign error: (x + 2) is a factor means f(−2) = 0, not f(2) = 0.
For a divisor like (2x − 1) substituting x = 2 instead of x = 1/2.
Leaving out zero coefficients in synthetic division: x³ − 7x + 6 must be written 1, 0, −7, 6.
Taking the product of roots of a cubic as d/a; it is −d/a.
Giving a constant remainder when dividing by a quadratic; it can be linear.
nsmqTips: Try x = 1 and x = −1 first; most quiz polynomials are built to factor with small integers.
When asked for an unknown coefficient, one substitution gives one linear equation; two factors give two equations.
Questions like 'find α² + β²' never need the roots themselves; quote sum and product aloud, then combine.

topics.summary: This topic covers solving linear, quadratic and simultaneous equations and finding the ranges of x that satisfy inequalities. NSMQ asks for roots, conditions on the discriminant, and solution intervals that must be stated quickly and precisely.
keyIdeas: The discriminant b² − 4ac decides the roots: positive gives two real roots, zero gives one repeated root, negative gives no real roots.
A quadratic with roots α and β is x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the sign.
For (x − α)(x − β) with α < β: the expression is negative between the roots and positive outside them.
Completing the square gives the turning point and the minimum or maximum value.
Squaring both sides can create false roots; always check in the original equation.
Two linear equations have a unique solution when their gradients differ.

formulas.name: Quadratic formula
formulas.note: For ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.

formulas.name: Discriminant
formulas.note: D > 0: two real roots; D = 0: equal roots; D < 0: no real roots; D a perfect square (rational coefficients): rational roots.

formulas.name: Completed square
formulas.formula: ax² + bx + c = a(x + b/2a)² + (4ac − b²)/4a
formulas.note: Turning point at x = −b/2a.

formulas.name: Extreme value
formulas.formula: Min (a > 0) or max (a < 0) of ax² + bx + c = (4ac − b²)/4a
formulas.note: Occurs at x = −b/2a.

formulas.name: Quadratic from roots
formulas.note: Multiply through to clear fractions.

formulas.name: Modulus inequalities
formulas.formula: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b ;  |x − a| > b ⇔ x < a − b or x > a + b

formulas.name: Quadratic inequality
formulas.formula: (x − α)(x − β) < 0 ⇔ α < x < β ;  (x − α)(x − β) > 0 ⇔ x < α or x > β
formulas.note: α < β and the x² coefficient is positive.

formulas.name: Unique solution of a linear system
formulas.formula: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ have one solution if a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0
formulas.note: If it is zero the lines are parallel (no solution) or the same line (infinitely many).

formulas.name: AM–GM inequality
formulas.note: Equality when a = b; gives maximum products and minimum sums.

shortcuts.name: a + b + c = 0
shortcuts.rule: If the coefficients add to zero, the roots are 1 and c/a. If a − b + c = 0, the roots are −1 and −c/a.

shortcuts.name: Sum–product factoring
shortcuts.rule: For x² − Sx + P, find two numbers adding to S and multiplying to P.

shortcuts.name: Reciprocal roots
shortcuts.rule: Reverse the coefficients: cx² + bx + a = 0 has roots 1/α and 1/β.
shortcuts.example: 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0 has roots 3 and 1/2, so 3x² − 7x + 2 = 0 has roots 1/3 and 2.

shortcuts.name: Symmetric simultaneous equations
shortcuts.rule: If x + y = S and xy = P, then x and y are the roots of t² − St + P = 0.

shortcuts.name: Test one point
shortcuts.rule: After finding the critical values, test x = 0 (or any easy value) to see which region works.
shortcuts.example: (x − 2)(x + 3) ≤ 0: at x = 0 the value is −6 ≤ 0, so the middle region works: −3 ≤ x ≤ 2.

shortcuts.name: Fixed sum, maximum product
shortcuts.rule: With x + y fixed, xy is greatest when x = y.
shortcuts.example: x + y = 20: maximum xy = 10 × 10 = 100. A 40 m fence encloses at most a 10 m × 10 m = 100 m² rectangle.

traps: Dividing both sides by x and losing the root x = 0: x² = 3x gives x = 0 or x = 3.
Forgetting to reverse the inequality sign when multiplying by a negative: −2x > 6 gives x < −3.
Not checking squared equations: √(x + 2) = x gives x = 2 or −1, but x = −1 fails because √1 ≠ −1.
Using b instead of −b in the quadratic formula when b is negative.
Writing 'x > −3 and x < 2' when the answer is the union of two outer regions.
nsmqTips: State inequality answers in full: say 'x is between −3 and 2 inclusive', not just the two numbers.
For 'find k so the equation has equal roots', set b² − 4ac = 0 at once; for 'real roots' use ≥ 0.
Spot a + b + c = 0 before reaching for the formula; quiz setters use it often.

topics.summary: Partial fractions split one rational expression into a sum of simpler fractions. The method is needed for integration, series summation and binomial expansions, and NSMQ often asks for a single coefficient that can be found almost instantly.
keyIdeas: A rational expression is proper when the numerator has a lower degree than the denominator; divide first if it is improper.
Each distinct linear factor (x − a) gives a term A/(x − a).
A repeated factor (x − a)² gives two terms: A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)².
An irreducible quadratic factor (x² + k, k > 0) gives (Bx + C)/(x² + k).
The cover-up rule gives the coefficient of a non-repeated linear factor at once.
Coefficients can be found by substituting convenient x values or by comparing coefficients.
Fractions such as 1/(r(r + 1)) split into differences, so sums telescope.

formulas.name: Distinct linear factors
formulas.note: a ≠ b.

formulas.name: Repeated linear factor
formulas.formula: (px + q)/(x − a)² = A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²
formulas.note: Every power up to the highest must appear.

formulas.name: Quadratic factor
formulas.formula: f(x)/((x − a)(x² + k)) = A/(x − a) + (Bx + C)/(x² + k)
formulas.note: The quadratic's numerator is linear, not constant.

formulas.name: Improper fraction
formulas.formula: If deg(numerator) ≥ deg(denominator): fraction = polynomial quotient + proper remainder fraction
formulas.note: Divide first, then split the remainder.

formulas.name: Cover-up rule
formulas.formula: Coefficient of 1/(x − a) = rest of the expression evaluated at x = a
formulas.note: Only for a non-repeated linear factor, or the highest power of a repeated one.

formulas.name: Difference of two linear factors
formulas.note: Instant split for a constant numerator.

formulas.name: Consecutive product
formulas.note: The basis of telescoping sums.

formulas.name: Telescoping sum
formulas.note: All middle terms cancel.

shortcuts.name: Cover-up
shortcuts.rule: Cover the factor (x − a), substitute x = a into what is left.

shortcuts.name: Check with x = 0
shortcuts.rule: Substitute x = 0 into both sides to confirm the answer.
shortcuts.example: For the example above: left side 1/(−2) = −0.5; right side 2/(−1) + 3/2 = −2 + 1.5 = −0.5. Correct.

shortcuts.name: Rewrite in powers of the repeated factor
shortcuts.rule: For a linear numerator over (x − a)², write the numerator as k(x − a) + c.

shortcuts.name: Large-x limit for the missing coefficient
shortcuts.rule: Multiply by x and let x grow large: leading terms give a relation between coefficients.
shortcuts.example: (2x² + x + 3)/((x + 1)(x² + 1)): cover-up gives A = 4/2 = 2; large x gives 2 = A + B, so B = 0; x = 0 gives 3 = A + C, so C = 1. Answer 2/(x + 1) + 1/(x² + 1).

shortcuts.name: Telescoping on sight
shortcuts.rule: Σ 1/(r(r + 1)) up to n is n/(n + 1).

shortcuts.name: Constant-numerator split
shortcuts.rule: For 1/((x − a)(x − b)), multiply the difference of the two simple fractions by 1/(a − b).

traps: Splitting an improper fraction without dividing first.
Writing only B/(x − a)² for a repeated factor and missing A/(x − a).
Putting a constant over an irreducible quadratic instead of Bx + C.
Using cover-up for the lower-power term of a repeated factor; it only gives the top-power coefficient.
Sign slips when substituting a negative root such as x = −2.
nsmqTips: Quiz questions often ask for one coefficient only; use cover-up and answer in seconds.
Confirm your answer by substituting x = 0 in your head before you speak.
Sums like 1/(1×3) + 1/(3×5) + … are telescoping in disguise: 1/((2r − 1)(2r + 1)) = ½[1/(2r − 1) − 1/(2r + 1)].

topics.summary: Sequences are ordered lists of numbers and series are their sums, mainly arithmetic progressions (AP) and geometric progressions (GP). NSMQ loves nth-term and sum questions that reward pattern spotting over long formulas.
keyIdeas: In an AP each term adds a common difference d; in a GP each term is multiplied by a common ratio r.
Three numbers a, b, c are in AP when 2b = a + c and in GP when b² = ac.
The sum of an AP equals the number of terms times the average of the first and last terms.
An infinite GP converges only when |r| < 1.
Any term can be found from the sums: aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.
Recurring decimals are infinite GPs and can be written as fractions.
Standard sums: Σr, Σr² and Σr³ have closed forms.

formulas.name: nth term of an AP
formulas.note: a is the first term, d the common difference.

formulas.name: Sum of an AP
formulas.note: l is the last term.

formulas.name: nth term of a GP
formulas.note: r is the common ratio.

formulas.name: Sum of a GP
formulas.note: r ≠ 1; use the second form when |r| < 1.

formulas.name: Sum to infinity
formulas.note: Only when |r| < 1.

formulas.name: Arithmetic and geometric means
formulas.note: AM ≥ GM for positive a, b.

formulas.name: Term from sums
formulas.note: Works for any sequence.

formulas.name: Sum of first n integers
formulas.note: r from 1 to n.

formulas.name: Sum of squares
formulas.note: r from 1 to n.

formulas.name: Sum of cubes
formulas.note: The square of the sum of the first n integers.

formulas.name: Sum of first n odd numbers
formulas.note: Quick check: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

shortcuts.name: Odd number of terms
shortcuts.rule: Sum = n × middle term

shortcuts.name: Pair from the ends
shortcuts.rule: Number of terms × average of first and last.
shortcuts.example: Multiples of 3 from 3 to 99: 33 terms, average (3 + 99)/2 = 51, sum = 33 × 51 = 1683.

shortcuts.name: Recurring decimal
shortcuts.rule: A block of k repeating digits after the point equals the block over k nines.

shortcuts.name: Read the AP from Sₙ
shortcuts.rule: If Sₙ = pn² + qn, then d = 2p and a = p + q.
shortcuts.example: Sₙ = 3n² + 2n: d = 6, a = 5, so aₙ = 6n − 1. Check: S₂ = 16 = 5 + 11.

shortcuts.name: Symmetric unknowns
shortcuts.rule: Take three AP terms as a − d, a, a + d (GP: a/r, a, ar) so the sum or product simplifies.
shortcuts.example: AP with sum 24 and product 440: 3a = 24 gives a = 8; 8(64 − d²) = 440 gives d² = 9, so the terms are 5, 8, 11.

traps: Miscounting terms: 5, 10, …, 50 has 10 terms, not 9; use n = (last − first)/d + 1.
Using S∞ when |r| ≥ 1; the series then has no finite sum.
Writing aₙ = a + nd or arⁿ instead of using n − 1.
Confusing the nth term with the sum of n terms.
Losing the sign when r is negative: the terms alternate in sign.
nsmqTips: Before using Sₙ, check if the number of terms is odd; the middle-term trick is faster.
For 'insert k means between a and b', the total number of terms is k + 2.
Say infinite GP answers as fractions; 0.333… = 1/3 is expected over a decimal.

topics.summary: The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ without multiplying out brackets, using combinations as coefficients. NSMQ asks for specific coefficients, terms independent of x, and quick approximations such as (1.02)⁵.
keyIdeas: The coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ are the numbers in row n of Pascal's triangle, ⁿC₀ to ⁿCₙ.
There are n + 1 terms, and the powers of a fall from n to 0 while powers of b rise from 0 to n.
The (r + 1)th term is ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ.
Coefficients are symmetric: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.
Substituting x = 1 gives the sum of the coefficients.
For negative or fractional n the expansion is infinite and valid only for |x| < 1 in (1 + x)ⁿ.
For small x, (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx.

formulas.name: Binomial expansion
formulas.formula: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, r = 0 to n
formulas.note: n a positive integer.

formulas.name: General term
formulas.note: Term number is r + 1.

formulas.name: Combination
formulas.note: Number of ways to choose r from n.

formulas.name: Symmetry
formulas.note: ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = 45.

formulas.name: Pascal's rule
formulas.note: Each entry is the sum of the two above it.

formulas.name: Sum of coefficients
formulas.note: Put a = b = 1.

formulas.name: Middle term
formulas.formula: n even: one middle term, the (n/2 + 1)th ;  n odd: two middle terms
formulas.note: The middle coefficient is the largest.

formulas.name: General binomial series
formulas.note: Any rational n; valid for |x| < 1.

formulas.name: Linear approximation
formulas.note: x small; add the x² term for more accuracy.

shortcuts.name: Term independent of x
shortcuts.rule: Write the power of x in the general term, set it to zero, solve for r.
shortcuts.example: (x² + 1/x)⁶: power is 2(6 − r) − r = 12 − 3r = 0, so r = 4 and the term is ⁶C₄ = 15.

shortcuts.name: Pick the coefficient directly
shortcuts.rule: Coefficient of xʳ in (1 + kx)ⁿ is ⁿCᵣ kʳ.

shortcuts.name: Sum of coefficients by x = 1
shortcuts.rule: Substitute x = 1 into the bracket.
shortcuts.example: Sum of coefficients of (3x − 2)⁷ is (3 − 2)⁷ = 1.

shortcuts.name: Small-x approximation
shortcuts.rule: Use 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2 and drop the rest.

shortcuts.name: Powers of 11 show Pascal rows
shortcuts.rule: Rows 0 to 4 of Pascal's triangle are the digits of 11⁰ to 11⁴.
shortcuts.example: 11⁴ = 14641, so (a + b)⁴ has coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

traps: Forgetting to raise the constant in the second term to the power r, or dropping its sign: in (x − 2)⁵ the x³ term is ⁵C₂ × (−2)² x³ = 40x³.
Off-by-one: the 5th term uses r = 4.
Expanding (4 + x)^(1/2) without first writing it as 2(1 + x/4)^(1/2); the series needs the form (1 + small).
Giving the term (80x³) when the coefficient (80) was asked, or the reverse.
Using an infinite expansion outside its range of validity |x| < 1.
nsmqTips: Say the general term aloud first; the rest is one line of arithmetic.
For approximations, state how many terms you used and round only at the end.
Memorise small combinations: ⁵C₂ = 10, ⁶C₃ = 20, ⁷C₃ = 35, ⁸C₄ = 70, ¹⁰C₃ = 120.

topics.summary: A function assigns exactly one output to each input; composites chain functions and inverses undo them. NSMQ questions test composite values, inverse formulas and domain or range restrictions, often with rational functions.
keyIdeas: A mapping is a function if every element of the domain has exactly one image.
A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one on its domain.
fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f.
The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.
Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f, and range of f⁻¹ = domain of f.
Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x) (symmetric about the y-axis); odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x) (symmetric about the origin).
Exclude values that make a denominator zero, a square root negative or a log argument non-positive.

formulas.name: Composite function
formulas.note: In general f∘g ≠ g∘f.

formulas.name: Inverse property
formulas.note: To find f⁻¹, write y = f(x), swap x and y, solve for y.

formulas.name: Inverse of a rational linear function
formulas.formula: f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d) ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (dx − b)/(−cx + a)
formulas.note: Swap a and d, change the signs of b and c.

formulas.name: Excluded values
formulas.formula: f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d): x ≠ −d/c and f(x) ≠ a/c
formulas.note: c ≠ 0; a/c is the horizontal asymptote.

formulas.name: Inverse of a composite
formulas.note: Undo in reverse order.

formulas.name: Even and odd tests
formulas.note: x² and cos x are even; x³ and sin x are odd.

formulas.name: Counting functions
formulas.formula: From a set of m elements to a set of n elements: nᵐ functions ;  n!/(n − m)! one-to-one functions
formulas.note: One-to-one count needs m ≤ n.

shortcuts.name: Rational inverse by swap-and-negate
shortcuts.rule: For (ax + b)/(cx + d), swap a and d and negate b and c.

shortcuts.name: Inverse value without the inverse
shortcuts.rule: To find f⁻¹(k), solve f(x) = k.

shortcuts.name: Range from the leading coefficients
shortcuts.rule: (ax + b)/(cx + d) can never equal a/c.
shortcuts.example: f(x) = (2x + 3)/(x − 4): domain x ≠ 4, range y ≠ 2.

shortcuts.name: Self-inverse pattern
shortcuts.rule: (ax + b)/(cx − a) is its own inverse, because swapping a and −a gives it back.
shortcuts.example: f(x) = (3x + 1)/(2x − 3) satisfies f⁻¹ = f, so f(f(5)) = 5 without any working.

shortcuts.name: Inside-out composites
shortcuts.rule: Evaluate the inner function at the number first; never build the general formula if a value is asked.

shortcuts.name: Count functions by choices
shortcuts.rule: Each of m inputs independently picks one of n outputs.
shortcuts.example: From {a, b, c} to {0, 1}: 2³ = 8 functions; none is one-to-one because 3 > 2.

traps: Treating f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x).
Applying functions in the wrong order: fg(x) means do g first.
Stating an inverse of x² without restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 (or x ≤ 0).
Forgetting the excluded value in the range of a rational function.
Calling a one-to-many relation a function.
nsmqTips: If only one value of a composite or inverse is asked, work with numbers, not formulas.
Memorise the swap-and-negate inverse; rational functions appear often.
When asked for a domain, say the excluded value clearly: 'all real x except 4'.

topics.summary: Sets organise objects into collections, logic studies how statements combine, and binary operations define new ways of combining two numbers. NSMQ uses Venn-diagram counts, truth values of implications, and identity and inverse elements of a defined operation.
keyIdeas: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, including the empty set and the set itself.
The empty set is a subset of every set.
De Morgan's laws turn the complement of a union into the intersection of complements, and the reverse.
An implication p → q is false only when p is true and q is false.
An implication is equivalent to its contrapositive, not to its converse or inverse.
A binary operation ∗ is commutative if a∗b = b∗a and associative if (a∗b)∗c = a∗(b∗c).
The identity e satisfies a∗e = e∗a = a; the inverse a⁻¹ satisfies a∗a⁻¹ = a⁻¹∗a = e.

formulas.name: Union of two sets
formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
formulas.note: Subtract the overlap counted twice.

formulas.name: Union of three sets
formulas.formula: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(B ∩ C) − n(A ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)
formulas.note: Inclusion–exclusion.

formulas.name: Complement
formulas.note: U is the universal set.

formulas.name: Subsets
formulas.note: n is the number of elements.

formulas.name: De Morgan's laws (sets)
formulas.note: Same pattern as logic.

formulas.name: De Morgan's laws (logic)
formulas.note: ∧ is 'and', ∨ is 'or', ¬ is 'not'.

formulas.name: Implication and contrapositive
formulas.note: Converse q → p and inverse ¬p → ¬q are equivalent to each other, not to p → q.

formulas.name: Truth table size
formulas.note: n is the number of simple statements.

formulas.name: Identity element
formulas.formula: a∗e = e∗a = a for all a
formulas.note: Must hold on both sides.

formulas.name: Inverse element
formulas.note: Find e first.

shortcuts.name: Additive operation a∗b = a + b + k
shortcuts.rule: Identity e = −k; inverse of a is −a − 2k.
shortcuts.example: a∗b = a + b − 3: e = 3, inverse of 5 is −5 + 6 = 1. Check: 5∗1 = 5 + 1 − 3 = 3.

shortcuts.name: Operation a∗b = a + b + kab
shortcuts.rule: Identity e = 0; inverse of a is −a/(1 + ka).
shortcuts.example: a∗b = a + b + 2ab: inverse of 3 is −3/7. Check: 3 − 3/7 − 18/7 = 3 − 3 = 0.

shortcuts.name: Neither from the union
shortcuts.rule: Neither = total − [n(A) + n(B) − both].
shortcuts.example: 50 students, 30 take A, 25 take B, 12 take both: union = 43, so neither = 7.

shortcuts.name: Exactly one of two
shortcuts.rule: Exactly one = n(A) + n(B) − 2 n(A ∩ B).
shortcuts.example: With the numbers above: 30 + 25 − 24 = 31 (also 43 − 12).

shortcuts.name: Symmetry means commutative
shortcuts.rule: If swapping a and b leaves the formula unchanged, the operation is commutative.
shortcuts.example: a∗b = a² + b² − ab is symmetric, so commutative; a∗b = a − 2b is not, since 1∗2 = −3 but 2∗1 = 0.

shortcuts.name: Contrapositive flip
shortcuts.rule: Negate both parts and reverse the arrow.
shortcuts.example: 'If a number is divisible by 4, it is even' is equivalent to 'If a number is not even, it is not divisible by 4'.

traps: Subtracting the intersection twice when computing a union.
Treating the converse as equivalent to the original statement.
Checking the identity on one side only; a∗e = a and e∗a = a are both required.
Thinking one example proves associativity; examples only disprove it.
Forgetting the empty set and the set itself when counting subsets.
nsmqTips: For Venn questions, start filling the diagram from the innermost overlap outward.
For binary operations, find the identity first and say it aloud; inverses follow in one step.
In logic riddles, an implication with a false hypothesis is automatically true.

topics.summary: Number theory studies whole numbers: primes, divisibility, HCF and LCM, number bases and remainders. Modular arithmetic gives remainders of huge powers quickly, a favourite NSMQ 'riddle' and speed-race question.
keyIdeas: Every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes; 1 is not a prime.
a ≡ b (mod n) means a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n.
Congruences can be added, subtracted, multiplied and raised to powers.
Last digits of powers repeat in cycles of length 1, 2 or 4.
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.
The Euclidean algorithm finds the HCF by repeated remainders.
A number in base b uses digits 0 to b − 1, and the place values are powers of b.

formulas.name: HCF and LCM
formulas.formula: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b
formulas.note: Two numbers only.

formulas.name: Number of divisors
formulas.formula: N = pᵃ qᵇ rᶜ ⇒ number of divisors = (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1)
formulas.note: p, q, r distinct primes.

formulas.name: Sum of divisors
formulas.formula: N = pᵃ qᵇ ⇒ σ(N) = (1 + p + … + pᵃ)(1 + q + … + qᵇ)
formulas.note: Includes 1 and N.

formulas.name: Euclidean algorithm
formulas.formula: HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, a mod b)
formulas.note: Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder is the HCF.

formulas.name: Congruence
formulas.formula: a ≡ b (mod n) ⇔ n divides (a − b)
formulas.note: Remainders are taken from 0 to n − 1.

formulas.name: Fermat's little theorem
formulas.note: p prime and p does not divide a.

formulas.name: Base conversion
formulas.formula: (dₖ…d₁d₀) in base b = dₖbᵏ + … + d₁b + d₀

formulas.name: Divisibility rules
formulas.formula: 3 or 9: digit sum divisible by 3 or 9 ;  11: alternating digit sum divisible by 11 ;  4: last two digits ;  8: last three digits
formulas.note: A number is divisible by 6 if divisible by 2 and 3.

formulas.name: Trailing zeros of n!
formulas.note: Counts factors of 5.

shortcuts.name: Last-digit cycles
shortcuts.rule: Find the cycle of last digits and reduce the exponent mod the cycle length (use the 4th term when the remainder is 0).
shortcuts.example: 7²⁰²⁶: 7, 9, 3, 1 repeats; 2026 = 4 × 506 + 2, so the last digit is 9.

shortcuts.name: Find a power that is 1
shortcuts.rule: Look for a small power ≡ 1, then split the exponent.
shortcuts.example: 2¹⁰⁰ mod 7: 2³ = 8 ≡ 1, and 100 = 3 × 33 + 1, so the remainder is 2.

shortcuts.name: Use −1
shortcuts.rule: If a ≡ −1 (mod n), then even powers give 1 and odd powers give −1.
shortcuts.example: 2¹⁰⁰ mod 3: 2 ≡ −1, so (−1)¹⁰⁰ = 1. And 10⁹⁹ mod 11: 10 ≡ −1, so the remainder is −1 ≡ 10.

shortcuts.name: Digit sum gives mod 9
shortcuts.rule: A number has the same remainder mod 9 as its digit sum.
shortcuts.example: 123456: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21 → 2 + 1 = 3, so the remainder on division by 9 is 3.

shortcuts.name: Divisor count from prime powers
shortcuts.rule: Add 1 to each exponent and multiply.

shortcuts.name: Euclid by subtraction
shortcuts.rule: Replace the larger number with its remainder until one divides the other.

traps: Applying HCF × LCM = product to three numbers; it holds only for two.
Calling 1 a prime, or forgetting that 2 is the only even prime.
Giving negative remainders: −7 mod 5 is 3, not −2.
Using the 0th cycle position: when the exponent is a multiple of 4, take the 4th last digit (for 7, that is 1).
Writing digits that are not allowed in a base, such as 8 in base 8.
nsmqTips: For remainders of large powers, look for a power equal to 1 or −1; this almost always exists.
Factor numbers into primes at once; divisor counts, HCF and LCM all follow.
In base problems, convert to base 10, do the arithmetic, then convert back, unless the numbers are tiny.

topics.summary: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that represents systems of equations and linear transformations. NSMQ asks for determinants, inverses, products and conditions for a matrix to be singular, usually with 2×2 or 3×3 matrices.
keyIdeas: Matrices can be multiplied only when the number of columns of the first equals the number of rows of the second.
Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB ≠ BA in general.
A square matrix is singular (has no inverse) exactly when its determinant is zero.
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.
Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant; a row of zeros or two proportional rows give zero.
|det A| is the area (2×2) or volume (3×3) scale factor of the transformation A.
A system AX = B has a unique solution X = A⁻¹B when det A ≠ 0.

formulas.name: Notation
formulas.formula: (a b; c d) means the 2×2 matrix with first row a, b and second row c, d
formulas.note: Semicolons separate rows.

formulas.name: 2×2 determinant
formulas.formula: det (a b; c d) = ad − bc
formulas.note: Leading diagonal product minus the other diagonal.

formulas.name: 2×2 inverse
formulas.note: Exists only if ad − bc ≠ 0.

formulas.name: 3×3 determinant (first row)
formulas.formula: det = a₁₁(a₂₂a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₂) − a₁₂(a₂₁a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₁) + a₁₃(a₂₁a₃₂ − a₂₂a₃₁)
formulas.note: Cofactor signs follow + − +.

formulas.name: Product dimensions
formulas.note: Inner sizes must match.

formulas.name: Determinant of a product
formulas.note: Also det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A.

formulas.name: Scalar multiple
formulas.note: A is n × n.

formulas.name: Transpose and inverse rules
formulas.note: Order reverses.

formulas.name: Triangle area
formulas.formula: Area = ½ |det (x₁ y₁ 1; x₂ y₂ 1; x₃ y₃ 1)|
formulas.note: Zero area means the points are collinear.

formulas.name: 2×2 eigenvalues
formulas.note: λ₁ + λ₂ = trace, λ₁λ₂ = det.

shortcuts.name: 2×2 inverse in one move
shortcuts.rule: Swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries, divide by the determinant.

shortcuts.name: Triangular matrix
shortcuts.rule: Multiply the diagonal entries.

shortcuts.name: Spot a zero determinant
shortcuts.rule: Look for a zero row, two equal rows or two proportional rows.

shortcuts.name: Rule of Sarrus
shortcuts.rule: For 3×3: sum of the three down-right diagonal products minus the three up-right diagonal products.

shortcuts.name: Scaling the determinant
shortcuts.rule: Each row scaled by k multiplies det by k, so the whole n × n matrix gives kⁿ.
shortcuts.example: A is 3×3 with det A = 5: det(2A) = 2³ × 5 = 40.

shortcuts.name: Eigenvalues from trace and determinant
shortcuts.rule: Find two numbers with sum = trace and product = det.

traps: Assuming AB = BA.
Multiplying by the determinant instead of dividing when forming an inverse.
Writing det(kA) = k det A for an n × n matrix.
Forgetting the minus sign on the middle cofactor in a 3×3 expansion.
Thinking det(A + B) = det A + det B.
nsmqTips: Check the determinant first; if it is zero the answer to 'find the inverse' is 'it does not exist'.
Expand a 3×3 determinant along the row or column with the most zeros.
For 'find k so the matrix is singular', set det = 0 and solve.

topics.summary: Complex numbers a + bi extend the reals so that every polynomial has roots, using i² = −1. At university level they are handled in polar and exponential form with De Moivre's theorem and roots of unity, all frequent NSMQ riddle material.
keyIdeas: i² = −1, and powers of i repeat in the cycle i, −1, −i, 1.
A complex number a + bi is the point (a, b) on the Argand diagram.
The modulus |z| is the distance from the origin; the argument is the angle from the positive real axis, usually taken in (−π, π].
Multiplying complex numbers multiplies moduli and adds arguments.
Non-real roots of polynomials with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs.
The n nth roots of a complex number are equally spaced on a circle, 2π/n apart.
Euler's formula links exponentials and trigonometry: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ.

formulas.name: Modulus
formulas.note: Distance from the origin.

formulas.name: Conjugate
formulas.formula: z̄ = a − bi ;  z z̄ = |z|² = a² + b²
formulas.note: Use the conjugate of the denominator to divide.

formulas.name: Division
formulas.note: Real denominator after multiplying.

formulas.name: Polar and exponential form
formulas.formula: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = re^(iθ)
formulas.note: r = |z|, θ = arg z; tan θ = b/a with the quadrant checked.

formulas.name: Products and quotients
formulas.formula: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| ;  arg(z₁z₂) = arg z₁ + arg z₂ ;  |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| ;  arg(z₁/z₂) = arg z₁ − arg z₂
formulas.note: Arguments may need adjusting by 2π.

formulas.name: De Moivre's theorem
formulas.formula: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ
formulas.note: So (re^(iθ))ⁿ = rⁿe^(inθ).

formulas.name: nth roots
formulas.note: Exactly n distinct roots.

formulas.name: Cube roots of unity
formulas.note: The nth roots of unity always sum to 0 for n ≥ 2.

formulas.name: Euler's identity
formulas.note: θ = π in Euler's formula.

formulas.name: Circle in the Argand plane
formulas.note: Circle with centre z₀ and radius r.

shortcuts.name: Powers of i
shortcuts.rule: Reduce the exponent mod 4: remainder 0, 1, 2, 3 gives 1, i, −1, −i.
shortcuts.example: i²⁰²⁷: 2027 = 4 × 506 + 3, so i²⁰²⁷ = −i.

shortcuts.name: (1 + i)² = 2i
shortcuts.rule: Square (1 + i) first, then raise 2i to the remaining power.

shortcuts.name: Square root by modulus
shortcuts.rule: For √(a + bi) = x + yi use x² − y² = a and x² + y² = |a + bi|, then the sign of b fixes the sign pairing.

shortcuts.name: Modulus of a quotient
shortcuts.rule: Divide the moduli instead of dividing the numbers.

shortcuts.name: Quadratic from a complex root
shortcuts.rule: For root p + qi of a real quadratic: x² − 2px + (p² + q²) = 0.
shortcuts.example: Root 2 + 3i: x² − 4x + 13 = 0.

shortcuts.name: Reduce powers of ω mod 3
shortcuts.rule: ω³ = 1, so only the exponent mod 3 matters; then use 1 + ω + ω² = 0.
shortcuts.example: 1 + ω¹⁰⁰ + ω²⁰⁰ = 1 + ω + ω² = 0, since 100 ≡ 1 and 200 ≡ 2 (mod 3).

traps: Taking the argument of −1 − i as π/4 from tan θ = 1; it lies in the third quadrant, so arg = −3π/4.
Writing |a + bi| = a + b instead of √(a² + b²).
Using √(−4) × √(−9) = √36 = 6; the correct value is 2i × 3i = −6.
Assuming conjugate roots when the polynomial has non-real coefficients.
Applying De Moivre without first writing z in polar form, or forgetting to raise the modulus to the power n.
nsmqTips: For large powers, change to polar form at once: (1 + i) = √2 e^(iπ/4) is the most common case.
State arguments in radians unless degrees are asked, and give the principal value.
For 'find the nth roots', say the first root and the spacing 2π/n; the rest follow.

topics.summary: Coordinate geometry describes points and lines with numbers, so distances, gradients and areas become algebra. NSMQ asks for equations of lines, perpendicular distances and areas of triangles that can be done in a few lines of mental work.
keyIdeas: The gradient is rise over run and equals tan θ, where θ is the angle the line makes with the positive x-axis.
Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1.
A vertical line x = k has undefined gradient; a horizontal line y = k has gradient 0.
The line ax + by + c = 0 has gradient −a/b and y-intercept −c/b.
Three points are collinear if the triangle they form has zero area.
The perpendicular from a point to a line gives the shortest distance.
The centroid of a triangle is the average of its vertices.

formulas.name: Distance
formulas.note: Between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂).

formulas.name: Midpoint
formulas.note: Average the coordinates.

formulas.name: Internal division
formulas.note: P divides AB in the ratio m : n from A(x₁, y₁) to B(x₂, y₂).

formulas.name: Gradient
formulas.note: x₁ ≠ x₂.

formulas.name: Point–gradient form
formulas.note: Line through (x₁, y₁) with gradient m.

formulas.name: Intercept form
formulas.note: x-intercept a, y-intercept b.

formulas.name: Parallel and perpendicular
formulas.note: Perpendicular gradient is −1/m.

formulas.name: Point-to-line distance
formulas.note: From (x₀, y₀) to ax + by + c = 0.

formulas.name: Distance between parallel lines
formulas.note: For ax + by + c₁ = 0 and ax + by + c₂ = 0.

formulas.name: Angle between two lines
formulas.note: Gives the acute angle; if m₁m₂ = −1 the lines are perpendicular.

formulas.name: Triangle area
formulas.formula: A = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|
formulas.note: Zero means collinear.

formulas.name: Centroid
formulas.note: Meeting point of the medians.

shortcuts.name: Perpendicular line by swapping coefficients
shortcuts.rule: A line perpendicular to ax + by = c is bx − ay = k; put in the point to find k.
shortcuts.example: Perpendicular to 3x + 4y = 7 through (1, 2): 4x − 3y = 4 − 6, so 4x − 3y = −2.

shortcuts.name: Parallel line by keeping coefficients
shortcuts.rule: A line parallel to ax + by = c is ax + by = k; put in the point to find k.
shortcuts.example: Parallel to 2x − 5y = 1 through (3, −1): 2(3) − 5(−1) = 11, so 2x − 5y = 11.

shortcuts.name: Pythagorean triples in distances
shortcuts.rule: Divide the differences by a common factor and look for 3-4-5, 5-12-13 or 8-15-17.
shortcuts.example: (1, 2) to (7, 10): differences 6 and 8 = 2 × (3, 4), so distance = 2 × 5 = 10.

shortcuts.name: Intercepts at a glance
shortcuts.rule: For ax + by = c, the intercepts are c/a and c/b; the triangle with the axes has area ½ × |c/a| × |c/b|.
shortcuts.example: 3x + 4y = 12: intercepts 4 and 3, area 6, and the segment between them has length 5.

shortcuts.name: Shoelace area
shortcuts.rule: Use the triangle-area formula as a single line of arithmetic.

shortcuts.name: Collinearity by ratios
shortcuts.rule: Points are collinear if the gradient between each pair is the same.
shortcuts.example: (1, 2), (3, 6), (5, 10): each gradient is 2, so they lie on y = 2x.

traps: Taking the perpendicular gradient as 1/m or −m instead of −1/m.
Mixing x₁ and x₂ in the section formula: the ratio number m multiplies the far point B.
Dropping the absolute value in the point-to-line distance and giving a negative length.
Reading the gradient of ax + by + c = 0 as a or −b/a; it is −a/b.
Treating a vertical line as having gradient 0.
nsmqTips: Keep lines in the form ax + by = c; parallel and perpendicular lines then come from coefficient tricks.
Before using the distance formula, look for a Pythagorean triple in the differences.
Say equations in a clean integer form such as 4x − 3y + 2 = 0 unless another form is asked.

topics.summary: This topic covers the equation of a circle and the three other conics (parabola, ellipse, hyperbola), which you get by slicing a cone at different angles. NSMQ riddles and speed rounds often ask for a centre, radius, focus, eccentricity or tangent length straight from an equation, so you need to read these off at a glance.
keyIdeas: A second-degree equation is a circle only if the x² and y² coefficients are equal and there is no xy term.
Divide through by the x² coefficient before reading off the centre and radius.
Eccentricity e sorts the conics: e = 0 circle, 0 < e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola.
The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent there.
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord cuts the chord in half.
An angle in a semicircle is 90°, and angles in the same segment are equal.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.
For an ellipse c² = a² − b²; for a hyperbola c² = a² + b².

formulas.name: Circle, centre–radius form
formulas.note: Centre (a, b), radius r.

formulas.name: Circle, general form
formulas.formula: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, centre (−g, −f), r = √(g² + f² − c)
formulas.note: Only valid once the x² and y² coefficients are both 1. A real circle needs g² + f² − c > 0.

formulas.name: Tangent to x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁)
formulas.note: Replace x² by x x₁ and y² by y y₁. For the general form: x x₁ + y y₁ + g(x + x₁) + f(y + y₁) + c = 0.

formulas.name: Length of tangent from external point (x₁, y₁)
formulas.note: Substitute the point into the left side of the general equation (coefficients of x² and y² equal to 1).

formulas.name: Chord length
formulas.note: d is the perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord.

formulas.name: Arc length and sector area
formulas.note: θ in radians. In degrees: s = (θ/360) × 2πr, A = (θ/360) × πr².

formulas.name: Parabola
formulas.formula: y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, latus rectum length 4a
formulas.note: For x² = 4ay the focus is (0, a) and the directrix is y = −a.

formulas.name: Ellipse
formulas.formula: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b): c² = a² − b², e = c/a, foci (±c, 0)
formulas.note: Vertices (±a, 0), area πab, directrices x = ±a/e.

formulas.name: Hyperbola
formulas.formula: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: c² = a² + b², e = c/a, foci (±c, 0), asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x
formulas.note: e > 1. The rectangular hyperbola xy = c² has e = √2.

formulas.name: Distance from point to line
formulas.note: Use it to test tangency: the line touches the circle when d = r.

shortcuts.name: Centre by halving and negating
shortcuts.rule: In x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 the centre is (−D/2, −E/2) and r² = (D/2)² + (E/2)² − F.

shortcuts.name: Plug in the point
shortcuts.rule: Substitute the point into the left side of the circle equation (in = 0 form). Negative means inside, zero means on, positive means outside. If it is positive, its square root is the tangent length.
shortcuts.example: Point (5, 4) and x² + y² − 2x − 4y − 4 = 0: 25 + 16 − 10 − 16 − 4 = 11 > 0, so the point is outside and the tangent length is √11.

shortcuts.name: Chord by Pythagorean triple
shortcuts.rule: The half-chord, the distance d and the radius r form a right triangle. Look for 3-4-5, 5-12-13 or 8-15-17.
shortcuts.example: r = 13 and the chord is 5 from the centre: the half-chord is 12, so the chord is 24.

shortcuts.name: Ellipse foci by triple
shortcuts.rule: c = √(a² − b²), which is often a triple. Then e = c/a.
shortcuts.example: x²/25 + y²/16 = 1: a = 5, b = 4, so c = 3, the foci are (±3, 0) and e = 3/5.

shortcuts.name: Parabola focus from 4a
shortcuts.rule: Divide the coefficient of x (or y) by 4 to get a.
shortcuts.example: y² = 12x: 4a = 12, a = 3, so the focus is (3, 0) and the directrix is x = −3. x² = 8y: a = 2, so the focus is (0, 2).

shortcuts.name: Hyperbola focus by triple
shortcuts.rule: c = √(a² + b²), which is again often a triple.
shortcuts.example: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1: c = 5, so the foci are (±5, 0), e = 5/3 and the asymptotes are y = ±(4/3)x.

traps: Reading the centre of 2x² + 2y² − 8x + 4y − 1 = 0 without first dividing by 2. The correct centre is (2, −1).
Getting the sign of the centre wrong: (x + 3)² means a = −3, not +3.
Using c² = a² − b² for a hyperbola, or c² = a² + b² for an ellipse.
Putting θ in degrees into s = rθ.
Giving r² when the question asks for r, or the reverse.
nsmqTips: Questions are often a bare equation followed by 'find the radius' or 'find the eccentricity'. Halve, negate and square in your head, and say only the final number.
For tangency questions, compare the distance from the centre to the line with r instead of solving simultaneous equations.
Memorise the eccentricity ranges. True/false and riddle clues often use 'e = 1'.

topics.summary: This topic covers angle facts, triangle and polygon properties, and the areas, surface areas and volumes of standard solids. It turns up across NSMQ rounds as quick-fire questions on polygon angles, Euler's formula and scale factors, all of which reward knowing standard results.
keyIdeas: The exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to 360°.
In a regular polygon, each interior angle plus each exterior angle equals 180°.
An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
Congruence tests: SSS, SAS, ASA (or AAS) and RHS. Similarity: AAA, sides in proportion, or SAS with the included sides in proportion.
If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.
Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 holds for every convex polyhedron.
The five Platonic solids have 4, 6, 8, 12 and 20 faces.
The midpoint theorem: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length.

formulas.name: Interior angle sum
formulas.note: n is the number of sides.

formulas.name: Each exterior angle (regular polygon)
formulas.note: Rearranged: n = 360°/exterior angle.

formulas.name: Number of diagonals
formulas.note: Each vertex joins to n − 3 others, and each diagonal is counted twice.

formulas.name: Triangle area (two sides and the included angle)
formulas.note: C is the angle between sides a and b.

formulas.name: Heron's formula
formulas.note: Use when all three sides are known.

formulas.name: Equilateral triangle and regular hexagon
formulas.note: A regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles.

formulas.name: Euler's polyhedron formula
formulas.note: V = vertices, E = edges, F = faces.

formulas.name: Cylinder
formulas.formula: V = πr²h, curved SA = 2πrh, total SA = 2πr(r + h)
formulas.note: Closed cylinder.

formulas.name: Cone
formulas.formula: V = ⅓πr²h, curved SA = πrl, l = √(r² + h²)
formulas.note: l is the slant height and h the vertical height.

formulas.name: Sphere and hemisphere
formulas.formula: Sphere V = (4/3)πr³, SA = 4πr². Solid hemisphere total SA = 3πr²
formulas.note: Hemisphere volume = (2/3)πr³.

formulas.name: Pyramid
formulas.note: Holds for any pyramid or cone.

formulas.name: Trapezium area
formulas.note: a and b are the parallel sides.

shortcuts.name: Sides from the interior angle
shortcuts.rule: Exterior = 180° − interior, then n = 360/exterior.
shortcuts.example: Each interior angle is 156°: exterior = 24°, so n = 360/24 = 15 sides.

shortcuts.name: Heron with nice triangles
shortcuts.rule: Memorise the 13-14-15 triangle (area 84) and the 5-5-6 triangle (area 12). Scaling the sides by k scales the area by k².

shortcuts.name: Scale-factor chain
shortcuts.rule: Take the square root of an area ratio or the cube root of a volume ratio to get the length ratio, then raise it to the power you need.
shortcuts.example: Similar solids with volumes 27 : 64: the length ratio is 3 : 4, so the surface area ratio is 9 : 16.

shortcuts.name: Edges from Euler
shortcuts.example: A solid with 12 faces and 20 vertices has E = 20 + 12 − 2 = 30 edges (the dodecahedron).

shortcuts.name: Diagonal count
shortcuts.rule: n(n − 3)/2. Know a few: pentagon 5, hexagon 9, octagon 20, decagon 35.
shortcuts.example: Decagon: 10 × 7/2 = 35 diagonals.

shortcuts.name: Sphere where V equals SA
shortcuts.rule: V/SA = r/3, so the volume and surface area are numerically equal when r = 3.
shortcuts.example: A sphere with SA = 36π has r = 3, so V = (4/3)π × 27 = 36π, the same number.

traps: Using the slant height l instead of the vertical height h in the cone volume.
Giving the curved surface area when the question asks for the total surface area (or the reverse).
Scaling the area by k instead of k² when lengths are scaled by k.
Using 360°/n for the interior angle. That gives the exterior angle.
Treating a hemisphere's total surface area as 2πr² and forgetting the flat circular face.
nsmqTips: Polygon riddles often give the ratio of interior to exterior angle. If the ratio is k : 1, then n = 2(k + 1). For example, 4 : 1 gives n = 10.
Know the V, E, F values of the Platonic solids: tetrahedron 4, 6, 4; cube 8, 12, 6; octahedron 6, 12, 8; dodecahedron 20, 30, 12; icosahedron 12, 30, 20.
Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal. It saves time and avoids rounding errors.

topics.summary: Trigonometry links angles to side ratios and covers identities, the sine and cosine rules, and trigonometric equations. It is one of the most heavily tested NSMQ maths areas, especially exact values, maximum and minimum values, and proving identities quickly.
keyIdeas: CAST tells you which ratios are positive: all in the 1st quadrant, sin in the 2nd, tan in the 3rd, cos in the 4th.
Complementary angles: sin θ = cos(90° − θ).
Radian conversion: π rad = 180°, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3°.
The range of a sin θ + b cos θ is from −√(a² + b²) to +√(a² + b²).
The sine rule has an ambiguous case (SSA): there can be two possible triangles.
The period of sin kx and cos kx is 360°/k; the period of tan kx is 180°/k.

formulas.name: Pythagorean identities
formulas.formula: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ
formulas.note: Divide the first by cos²θ or sin²θ to get the other two.

formulas.name: Compound angles (sine)
formulas.formula: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
formulas.note: The sign matches the sign in the bracket.

formulas.name: Compound angles (cosine)
formulas.formula: cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B
formulas.note: The sign flips.

formulas.name: Compound angles (tangent)
formulas.formula: tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B)
formulas.note: Undefined when the denominator is 0.

formulas.name: Double angle
formulas.formula: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A; tan 2A = 2tan A/(1 − tan²A)
formulas.note: Pick the form of cos 2A that leaves only one ratio.

formulas.name: Sine rule
formulas.formula: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R
formulas.note: R is the circumradius. Use it with two angles and a side, or two sides and a non-included angle.

formulas.name: Cosine rule
formulas.note: Use it with three sides, or two sides and the included angle.

formulas.name: Harmonic form
formulas.formula: a sin θ + b cos θ = R sin(θ + α), R = √(a² + b²), tan α = b/a
formulas.note: Maximum R, minimum −R.

formulas.name: General solutions
formulas.formula: sin θ = sin α → θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿα; cos θ = cos α → θ = 2nπ ± α; tan θ = tan α → θ = nπ + α
formulas.note: n is any integer, θ in radians.

formulas.name: Sum to product
formulas.formula: sin A + sin B = 2 sin[(A + B)/2] cos[(A − B)/2]; cos A + cos B = 2 cos[(A + B)/2] cos[(A − B)/2]
formulas.note: Useful for solving equations such as sin 3x + sin x = 0.

shortcuts.name: Square-root pattern for exact sines
shortcuts.rule: sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° = √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. Cosine is the same list in reverse. Fix the sign with CAST.
shortcuts.example: sin 240°: reference angle 60°, third quadrant (only tan positive), so sin 240° = −√3/2.

shortcuts.name: Max and min by triple
shortcuts.rule: The maximum of a sin θ + b cos θ is √(a² + b²). Spot the 3-4-5 or 5-12-13 triple.
shortcuts.example: The maximum of 7 − (3 sin θ + 4 cos θ) is 7 − (−5) = 12, and the minimum is 7 − 5 = 2.

shortcuts.name: Ratios from a triple
shortcuts.rule: Given one ratio of an acute angle, draw the triple triangle to read off the others.
shortcuts.example: sin θ = 5/13 with θ acute: cos θ = 12/13 and tan θ = 5/12. If θ is obtuse, cos θ = −12/13.

shortcuts.name: Cosine rule at 60° and 120°
shortcuts.rule: At 60°: c² = a² + b² − ab. At 120°: c² = a² + b² + ab.
shortcuts.example: Sides 5 and 8 with 60° between them: c² = 25 + 64 − 40 = 49, so c = 7. Sides 3 and 5 with 120° between them: c² = 9 + 25 + 15 = 49, so c = 7.

shortcuts.name: Period and amplitude at sight
shortcuts.rule: For y = A sin(kx) + D, the amplitude is |A|, the period is 360°/k, and the range is D − |A| to D + |A|.
shortcuts.example: y = 3 sin 4x + 1: amplitude 3, period 90°, range −2 to 4.

traps: Leaving the calculator in degree mode when the question uses radians (or the reverse).
Writing sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B.
Dividing both sides by cos θ (or sin θ) and losing the solutions where it equals 0. Factorise instead.
Missing the second triangle in the ambiguous SSA case of the sine rule.
Confusing sin²θ, which is (sin θ)², with sin(θ²).
nsmqTips: Simplify before you compute. For example, sin²20° + sin²70° = sin²20° + cos²20° = 1 straight away.
Many 'find the value' questions are standard identities in disguise. Look for complementary angles, double angles or the Pythagorean identities.
For maximum and minimum questions, give both the extreme value and the angle where it occurs if asked.

topics.summary: Vectors carry both magnitude and direction. This topic covers their algebra in 2D and 3D: magnitude, unit vectors, dot and cross products, and the section formula. NSMQ asks for quick magnitudes, perpendicularity conditions and areas, which are much faster with the shortcuts below.
keyIdeas: The displacement from A to B is AB = b − a, where a and b are position vectors.
Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is 0.
Two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other; then their cross product is 0.
The dot product gives a scalar and the cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both.
a × b = −(b × a): the cross product is not commutative.
i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j. Going the other way round gives a minus sign.
|a × b| is the area of the parallelogram formed by a and b.

formulas.name: Magnitude
formulas.note: For a = xi + yj + zk.

formulas.name: Unit vector
formulas.note: Same direction as a, length 1.

formulas.name: Dot product
formulas.formula: a·b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃
formulas.note: Gives the angle between vectors: cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|).

formulas.name: Cross product
formulas.formula: a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂)i + (a₃b₁ − a₁b₃)j + (a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)k, |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ
formulas.note: Works best as a 3 × 3 determinant with i, j, k in the top row.

formulas.name: Section formula (internal)
formulas.note: P divides AB in the ratio m : n. Note the cross-over: a is multiplied by n, the far part of the ratio.

formulas.name: Midpoint and centroid
formulas.note: Average the components.

formulas.name: Scalar projection
formulas.formula: Projection of a onto b = a·b/|b|
formulas.note: Vector projection = (a·b/|b|²) b.

formulas.name: Triangle area
formulas.formula: Area = ½|AB × AC|; in 2D, ½|x₁y₂ − x₂y₁|
formulas.note: For sides AB = (x₁, y₁) and AC = (x₂, y₂).

formulas.name: Vector equation of a line
formulas.note: a is a point on the line and d its direction vector.

formulas.name: Scalar triple product
formulas.note: Zero means a, b and c lie in one plane.

shortcuts.name: Pythagorean quadruples
shortcuts.example: |2i − 3j + 6k| = √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7, so the unit vector is (2i − 3j + 6k)/7.

shortcuts.name: Solve for k with the dot product
shortcuts.rule: Set the dot product to 0 and solve the linear equation.
shortcuts.example: (2, k, 3) perpendicular to (4, −2, 1): 8 − 2k + 3 = 0, so k = 5.5.

shortcuts.name: Centroid by averaging
shortcuts.rule: Add the x-components and divide by 3, then do the same for y.

shortcuts.name: 2D area by cross-multiplication
shortcuts.rule: Area = ½|x₁y₂ − x₂y₁| for two side vectors from the same vertex.
shortcuts.example: Sides (3, 1) and (1, 4): area = ½|12 − 1| = 5.5 square units.

shortcuts.name: Collinearity by ratio
shortcuts.rule: Check whether AC is a multiple of AB, component by component.
shortcuts.example: A(1, 1), B(3, 5), C(6, 11): AB = (2, 4) and AC = (5, 10) = 2.5 AB, so the points are collinear.

shortcuts.name: Cyclic order for unit vectors
shortcuts.rule: Read i → j → k → i round a circle. Going forwards is +, going backwards is −. Any vector crossed with itself gives 0.

traps: Writing AB = a − b instead of b − a.
Giving a vector answer for a dot product, or a scalar answer for a cross product.
Swapping the weights in the section formula. For ratio m : n, a is multiplied by n.
Measuring the angle between vectors placed head-to-tail. Both vectors must start from the same point.
Forgetting the minus sign on the j component when expanding the cross-product determinant.
nsmqTips: Questions often give two vectors with a parameter and ask when they are perpendicular or parallel. Set up one equation and solve it in one line.
Check whether the numbers form a Pythagorean quadruple before you start on a square root.
For 'find the unit vector', say the components over the magnitude clearly, e.g. '(3i + 4j)/5'.

topics.summary: Differentiation measures the instantaneous rate of change: gradients, velocities and turning points. In NSMQ you must differentiate standard functions in seconds and apply the result to tangents, maximum and minimum problems, and connected rates of change.
keyIdeas: dy/dx is the gradient of the tangent at a point.
At a stationary point dy/dx = 0. If d²y/dx² > 0 it is a minimum, and if d²y/dx² < 0 it is a maximum.
If d²y/dx² = 0 the test fails. Check the sign of dy/dx on either side.
The gradients of a tangent and the normal at the same point multiply to −1.
Velocity v = ds/dt and acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt².
A function is increasing where f'(x) > 0 and decreasing where f'(x) < 0.
Connected rates of change link through the chain rule: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt).

formulas.name: Power rule
formulas.note: Works for any real n, e.g. d/dx √x = 1/(2√x).

formulas.name: Product rule
formulas.note: For a product of two functions.

formulas.name: Quotient rule
formulas.note: The order of the numerator matters.

formulas.name: Chain rule
formulas.note: For composite functions: differentiate the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

formulas.name: Trigonometric derivatives
formulas.formula: d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = −sin x, d/dx tan x = sec²x
formulas.note: x in radians.

formulas.name: Exponential and logarithm
formulas.formula: d/dx eˣ = eˣ, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a
formulas.note: Also d/dx ln f(x) = f'(x)/f(x).

formulas.name: Equation of tangent
formulas.formula: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), m = f'(x₁)
formulas.note: The normal has gradient −1/m.

formulas.name: Small changes
formulas.note: Percentage error in xⁿ ≈ n × percentage error in x.

formulas.name: Connected rates
formulas.note: For example, a circle: dA/dt = 2πr dr/dt. A sphere: dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt.

formulas.name: First principles
formulas.note: The definition of the derivative.

shortcuts.name: Vertex of a quadratic
shortcuts.rule: The turning point of ax² + bx + c is at x = −b/(2a). It is a minimum if a > 0 and a maximum if a < 0.

shortcuts.name: Bracket power in one line
shortcuts.rule: d/dx [f(x)]ⁿ = n[f(x)]ⁿ⁻¹ f'(x).

shortcuts.name: Log of a function
shortcuts.rule: d/dx ln f(x) = f'(x)/f(x): the derivative of the inside over the inside.
shortcuts.example: d/dx ln(x² + 5x) = (2x + 5)/(x² + 5x). And d/dx ln(7x) = 1/x, because the 7 cancels.

shortcuts.name: Linear inside pops out
shortcuts.rule: If the inside is kx + c, just multiply by k.
shortcuts.example: d/dx sin 5x = 5 cos 5x, d/dx e^(3x) = 3e^(3x), d/dx (2x − 1)⁴ = 8(2x − 1)³.

shortcuts.name: Percentage error by the power
shortcuts.rule: If y = kxⁿ, then a p% error in x gives about an n·p% error in y.
shortcuts.example: The radius of a sphere is measured with a 2% error, so the volume (∝ r³) has about a 6% error.

shortcuts.name: Fixed sum gives maximum product at the halves
shortcuts.rule: If x + y = S, then xy is largest when x = y = S/2. A fixed perimeter gives the largest rectangle as a square.
shortcuts.example: Two numbers summing to 30 have maximum product 15 × 15 = 225. A 40 m fence encloses at most 10 × 10 = 100 m².

traps: Writing the quotient rule numerator as uv' − u'v, which gives the sign the wrong way round.
Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inside in the chain rule.
Assuming f''(x) = 0 always means a point of inflection.
Splitting ln(a + b) into ln a + ln b. Only ln(ab) splits like that.
Using the tangent gradient for the normal instead of −1/m.
nsmqTips: Questions often ask for the gradient at a point. Differentiate in your head, substitute, and say only the number.
For maximum and minimum word problems, write the quantity as a function of one variable first. Then look for symmetry, such as squares or equal parts.
With rates of change, give units, e.g. cm²/s. Quizmasters may ask.

topics.summary: Integration reverses differentiation. Applied as a definite integral, it gives areas, volumes of revolution, and displacement from velocity. NSMQ tests quick antiderivatives, symmetry arguments and standard area results.
keyIdeas: An indefinite integral always needs + C.
A definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative. To find total area, split the integral at the roots.
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ᵦᵃ f(x) dx, and ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0.
For an odd function, ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0. For an even function it equals 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.
Displacement = ∫ v dt and velocity = ∫ a dt.
When you substitute in a definite integral, change the limits as well.

formulas.name: Power rule
formulas.note: For n = −1 use the log rule.

formulas.name: Reciprocal
formulas.note: Keep the modulus.

formulas.name: Exponential
formulas.note: Divide by the coefficient of x.

formulas.name: Trigonometric
formulas.formula: ∫ sin kx dx = −cos kx/k + C, ∫ cos kx dx = sin kx/k + C, ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + C
formulas.note: x in radians.

formulas.name: Log pattern
formulas.note: Use when the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, or a constant multiple of it.

formulas.name: Integration by parts
formulas.note: Choose u by LIATE: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential.

formulas.name: Area under and between curves
formulas.formula: A = ∫ₐᵇ y dx; between curves A = ∫ₐᵇ (f − g) dx with f on top
formulas.note: Split the integral at points where the curves cross.

formulas.name: Volume of revolution
formulas.formula: About the x-axis V = π ∫ₐᵇ y² dx; about the y-axis V = π ∫ x² dy
formulas.note: Don't forget π.

formulas.name: Mean value of a function
formulas.note: The average height of the curve over the interval.

shortcuts.name: Parabola segment area
shortcuts.rule: The area between y = ax² + bx + c and a straight line (or the x-axis) crossing it at x = α and x = β is |a|(β − α)³/6.
shortcuts.example: y = x(4 − x) and the x-axis: a = −1, roots 0 and 4, so the area is 4³/6 = 64/6 = 32/3. Check: ∫₀⁴ (4x − x²) dx = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3.

shortcuts.name: Odd function vanishes
shortcuts.rule: Over limits −a to a, odd powers integrate to 0. Even powers give twice the integral from 0 to a.

shortcuts.name: Spot derivative over function
shortcuts.rule: If the numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, the answer is a log.
shortcuts.example: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx = ln(x² + 1) + C. ∫ x/(x² + 1) dx = ½ ln(x² + 1) + C.

shortcuts.name: Reverse chain for a linear inside
shortcuts.rule: Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power and by the coefficient of x.

shortcuts.name: Standard sine areas
shortcuts.rule: ∫₀^(π/2) sin x dx = 1 and ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2. The same holds for cos x over a matching quarter or half wave.
shortcuts.example: The area under one arch of y = 3 sin x is 3 × 2 = 6.

shortcuts.name: x times eˣ pattern
shortcuts.rule: ∫ x eˣ dx = (x − 1)eˣ + C. More generally, ∫ x e^(kx) dx = e^(kx)(x/k − 1/k²) + C.
shortcuts.example: ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx = [(x − 1)eˣ]₀¹ = 0 − (−1) = 1.

traps: Leaving out + C on an indefinite integral.
Using the power rule for x⁻¹, which would mean dividing by zero.
Forgetting to divide by k when integrating e^(kx), sin kx or cos kx.
Integrating straight across a root and letting the negative area cancel the positive area.
Leaving π out of volume-of-revolution answers, or squaring y incorrectly.
nsmqTips: Check for symmetry before you integrate. Odd integrands over symmetric limits give 0 instantly.
For the area between a parabola and a line, find the roots and use |a|(β − α)³/6. It takes seconds.
Check your antiderivative by differentiating it in your head before you answer.

topics.summary: A limit describes the value a function approaches. Continuity means there are no breaks, jumps or holes. This is first-year university analysis, and NSMQ uses it as tough riddles and problems built on standard limits, L'Hôpital's rule and continuity conditions.
keyIdeas: lim (x → a) f(x) exists only if the left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are equal.
f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined and lim (x → a) f(x) = f(a).
The indeterminate forms are 0/0, ∞/∞, 0 × ∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰ and ∞⁰.
Polynomials, eˣ, sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere. Rational functions are continuous except where the denominator is 0.
Differentiable implies continuous, but not the other way round: |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.
Intermediate value theorem: a continuous f on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b).
Squeeze theorem: if g ≤ f ≤ h and g and h have the same limit L, then f has limit L.

formulas.name: Fundamental trigonometric limit
formulas.note: x in radians. Also lim tan x / x = 1.

formulas.name: Cosine limit
formulas.note: Comes from 1 − cos x ≈ x²/2.

formulas.name: Definition of e
formulas.note: The standard 1^∞ form.

formulas.name: Exponential and log limits
formulas.formula: lim (x → 0) (eˣ − 1)/x = 1; lim (x → 0) ln(1 + x)/x = 1; lim (x → 0) (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a
formulas.note: Small-x approximations.

formulas.name: Power difference
formulas.formula: lim (x → a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹
formulas.note: This is the derivative of xⁿ at a.

formulas.name: L'Hôpital's rule
formulas.formula: If f/g → 0/0 or ∞/∞, then lim f/g = lim f'/g'
formulas.note: Differentiate the top and bottom separately, not with the quotient rule. Repeat if still indeterminate.

formulas.name: Rational function at infinity
formulas.formula: lim (x → ∞) P(x)/Q(x) = ratio of leading coefficients if the degrees are equal; 0 if deg P < deg Q; ±∞ if deg P > deg Q
formulas.note: Compare degrees first.

formulas.name: Continuity condition
formulas.formula: lim (x → a⁻) f = lim (x → a⁺) f = f(a)
formulas.note: Use it to find unknown constants in piecewise functions.

formulas.name: Growth hierarchy
formulas.formula: As x → ∞: ln x ≪ xⁿ ≪ eˣ ≪ x!
formulas.note: For example lim xⁿ/eˣ = 0 and lim ln x / x = 0.

shortcuts.name: Degree comparison
shortcuts.rule: For x → ∞, keep only the highest powers on the top and bottom.

shortcuts.name: Small-angle swap
shortcuts.rule: As x → 0, replace sin(kx) and tan(kx) by kx.
shortcuts.example: lim sin 5x / sin 2x = 5x/2x = 5/2. lim tan 3x / x = 3.

shortcuts.name: Power difference pattern
shortcuts.rule: (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → n aⁿ⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Spot a hidden derivative
shortcuts.rule: [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h is just f'(a), so skip the conjugate algebra.
shortcuts.example: lim (x → 0) (√(x + 9) − 3)/x is the derivative of √t at t = 9, which is 1/(2 × 3) = 1/6.

shortcuts.name: Match the pieces
shortcuts.rule: For continuity at the join, set the two formulas equal at the boundary point.
shortcuts.example: f(x) = kx + 1 for x < 2 and x² for x ≥ 2: continuity needs 2k + 1 = 4, so k = 3/2.

traps: Applying L'Hôpital when the limit is not 0/0 or ∞/∞, which gives a wrong answer.
Using the quotient rule inside L'Hôpital instead of differentiating the numerator and denominator separately.
Using sin x / x → 1 with x in degrees. It only holds in radians.
Assuming 1^∞ = 1. It is indeterminate and often equals a power of e.
Ignoring one-sided behaviour, e.g. |x|/x has no limit at 0 because the two sides give −1 and +1.
nsmqTips: First substitute directly. If you get a number, that is the answer. Only an indeterminate form needs the tricks.
Most quiz limits are one of about six standard forms: sin x/x, (1 + k/n)ⁿ, (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a), (eˣ − 1)/x, degree comparison, or a hidden derivative. Identify which one first.
For piecewise continuity riddles, set up one equation at the boundary and solve it out loud.

topics.summary: A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives. This topic covers first-order separable and linear equations, growth and decay models, and second-order constant-coefficient equations. It reaches university level and appears in NSMQ as recognition questions: identify the type, read off the solution, or check a proposed solution.
keyIdeas: The order is the highest derivative present. The degree is the power of that highest derivative once the equation is free of radicals and fractions in the derivatives.
A general solution of an nth-order equation has n arbitrary constants.
Separable equations: put all the y terms with dy and all the x terms with dx, then integrate both sides.
dN/dt = kN gives exponential growth (k > 0) or decay (k < 0).
For ay'' + by' + cy = 0, try y = e^(mx). This gives the auxiliary equation am² + bm + c = 0.
For a non-homogeneous equation, general solution = complementary function + particular integral.
Initial or boundary conditions fix the arbitrary constants.

formulas.name: Separable equation
formulas.note: Add the constant on one side straight after integrating.

formulas.name: Linear first-order
formulas.formula: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x); IF = e^(∫P dx); y × IF = ∫ Q × IF dx
formulas.note: IF stands for integrating factor. P is the coefficient of y once dy/dx has coefficient 1.

formulas.name: Exponential growth or decay
formulas.note: Half-life (k < 0) or doubling time (k > 0) = ln 2/|k|.

formulas.name: Newton's law of cooling
formulas.note: Tₛ is the surrounding temperature.

formulas.name: Second order, distinct real roots
formulas.formula: m₁ ≠ m₂ real: y = A e^(m₁x) + B e^(m₂x)
formulas.note: From am² + bm + c = 0 with b² − 4ac > 0.

formulas.name: Second order, repeated root
formulas.note: b² − 4ac = 0.

formulas.name: Second order, complex roots
formulas.formula: m = α ± iβ: y = e^(αx)(A cos βx + B sin βx)
formulas.note: b² − 4ac < 0.

formulas.name: Simple harmonic motion
formulas.formula: y'' + ω²y = 0 → y = A cos ωx + B sin ωx
formulas.note: Period 2π/ω.

formulas.name: Logistic growth
formulas.note: P → K (the carrying capacity) as t → ∞. Growth is fastest at P = K/2.

shortcuts.name: Read roots by factor pairs
shortcuts.rule: For y'' − sy' + py = 0, find two numbers with sum s and product p.
shortcuts.example: y'' − 5y' + 6y = 0: roots 2 and 3, so y = Ae^(2x) + Be^(3x).

shortcuts.name: Check a solution through the auxiliary equation
shortcuts.rule: y = e^(mx) solves the equation exactly when m satisfies am² + bm + c = 0. Just substitute m.
shortcuts.example: Is y = e^(−2x) a solution of y'' + y' − 2y = 0? m = −2: 4 − 2 − 2 = 0, so yes.

shortcuts.name: SHM at sight
shortcuts.rule: y'' + ky = 0 with k > 0 means ω = √k and period 2π/√k.
shortcuts.example: y'' + 9y = 0: ω = 3, y = A cos 3x + B sin 3x, period 2π/3.

shortcuts.name: Half-life with 0.693
shortcuts.example: Decay constant 0.1 per year gives t½ ≈ 6.93 years. After 3 half-lives, 1/8 remains.

shortcuts.name: Constant right-hand side
shortcuts.rule: For ay'' + by' + cy = K with c ≠ 0, the particular integral is y = K/c.

shortcuts.name: Limiting behaviour
shortcuts.rule: As t → ∞, decaying exponentials vanish, leaving the steady state.
shortcuts.example: Tea at 90 °C in a 30 °C room cools towards 30 °C. Logistic growth with K = 500 levels off at 500.

traps: Adding the constant at the end after dividing or taking logs. ln y = x + C gives y = Ae^x, not e^x + C.
Forgetting to make the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1 before finding P for the integrating factor.
Writing Ae^(mx) + Be^(mx) for a repeated root. The answer must be (A + Bx)e^(mx).
Leaving i in the final answer for complex roots instead of using cos and sin.
Confusing order with degree. (y')³ + y'' = 0 has order 2 and degree 1.
nsmqTips: Many quiz items ask for the order, the degree or the number of arbitrary constants. Answer instantly from the highest derivative.
For second-order equations, say the auxiliary equation, its roots and then the solution. That is three short steps.
Verifying a proposed solution is faster than solving. Substitute and check whether you get zero.

topics.summary: Statistics summarises data with measures of centre (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, variance, standard deviation), alongside graphs and rank correlation. NSMQ tests quick calculations with small data sets and how statistics change when data are transformed.
keyIdeas: Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean, median and mode but leaves the range, variance and SD unchanged.
Multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean and SD by |k| and the variance by k².
The median is the middle value of ordered data. With an even count, average the two middle values.
The mean is pulled towards outliers. The median resists them.
In a positively skewed distribution, typically mode < median < mean.
Use class boundaries, not class limits, for grouped data and histograms.
A histogram's bar area represents frequency, so frequency density = frequency/class width.

formulas.name: Mean
formulas.note: Use class midpoints for grouped data.

formulas.name: Assumed mean
formulas.formula: x̄ = A + Σfd/Σf, d = x − A
formulas.note: Choose A near the centre to keep the numbers small.

formulas.name: Variance
formulas.note: Population form, standard at SHS. The sample variance divides by n − 1.

formulas.name: Standard deviation
formulas.note: The square root of the variance.

formulas.name: Median position
formulas.note: For ordered raw data.

formulas.name: Grouped median
formulas.note: L = lower class boundary, F = cumulative frequency before the class, f = class frequency, c = class width.

formulas.name: Grouped mode
formulas.note: d₁ = modal frequency minus the previous class frequency, d₂ = modal frequency minus the next class frequency.

formulas.name: Coding
formulas.formula: y = (x − a)/b → ȳ = (x̄ − a)/b, σ_y = σ_x/|b|
formulas.note: Decode with x̄ = a + bȳ and σ_x = |b|σ_y.

formulas.name: Interquartile range
formulas.note: Semi-interquartile range = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2.

formulas.name: Spearman's rank correlation
formulas.note: d is the difference in ranks. −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1.

formulas.name: Pie chart sector
formulas.note: Each sector is proportional to its frequency.

shortcuts.name: Transform rule
shortcuts.rule: y = kx + c gives mean k x̄ + c and SD |k|σ. Adding c does not change the SD.
shortcuts.example: Mean 12 and SD 3. Each value is doubled and then 5 is added: new mean 29, new SD 6, new variance 36.

shortcuts.name: Consecutive integers
shortcuts.rule: The mean of an arithmetic sequence is (first + last)/2. The variance of 1, 2, …, n is (n² − 1)/12.
shortcuts.example: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: mean 3, variance (25 − 1)/12 = 2. Check: squared deviations 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 sum to 10, and 10/5 = 2.

shortcuts.name: Missing value from the mean
shortcuts.rule: Missing value = (mean × count) − sum of the known values.
shortcuts.example: Five numbers have mean 8 and four of them are 6, 7, 9, 10: the fifth is 40 − 32 = 8.

shortcuts.name: Deviations that cancel
shortcuts.rule: Pick a central A. If the deviations sum to 0, the mean is A.
shortcuts.example: 47, 52, 49, 55, 47 with A = 50: deviations −3, 2, −1, 5, −3 sum to 0, so the mean is 50.

shortcuts.name: SD of two values
shortcuts.rule: For two values the population SD is half their difference.
shortcuts.example: 4 and 10: mean 7, each is 3 away, so σ = 3.

shortcuts.name: Degrees per item
shortcuts.rule: Work out 360/total once, then multiply each frequency by it.
shortcuts.example: 72 students, so each student is 5°. 18 who like maths get 18 × 5 = 90°.

traps: Finding the median without ordering the data first.
Mixing up variance and SD, or forgetting to take the square root.
Thinking that adding a constant changes the SD.
Using class limits instead of class boundaries in grouped formulas.
Dividing by n − 1 when the question expects the population formula (or the reverse). Check the convention.
nsmqTips: Speed-round items use 3–6 numbers. Use an assumed mean or the symmetry of the data instead of adding everything up.
Transformation questions ('each score is increased by 5 and doubled') are common. Apply the operations in order to the mean, but only the scaling to the SD.
Say whether you are giving the variance or the SD so the answer is not misread.

topics.summary: Probability measures how likely events are, using sample spaces, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability and the binomial distribution. NSMQ draws heavily on dice, coins, cards and bags of balls, so the standard counts and complement tricks are essential.
keyIdeas: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, and the probabilities of all outcomes in the sample space add up to 1.
Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen: P(A ∩ B) = 0.
Independent events do not affect each other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
