Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
Without replacement, the denominator drops by 1 at each draw.
A standard deck has 52 cards: 4 suits of 13, 26 red, and 12 face cards (J, Q, K).
Two dice give 36 equally likely ordered outcomes; n coins give 2ⁿ outcomes.

formulas.name: Classical probability
formulas.note: Only valid when all outcomes are equally likely.

formulas.name: Complement
formulas.note: Use for 'at least one' questions.

formulas.name: Addition rule
formulas.formula: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
formulas.note: For mutually exclusive events, drop the last term.

formulas.name: Multiplication rule (independent)
formulas.note: This can also serve as a test for independence.

formulas.name: Conditional probability
formulas.note: The probability of A given that B has occurred.

formulas.name: Bayes' theorem
formulas.note: Reverses the direction of a conditional probability.

formulas.name: Binomial probability
formulas.formula: P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ, q = 1 − p
formulas.note: n independent trials, each with the same success probability p.

formulas.name: Binomial mean and variance
formulas.note: SD = √(npq).

formulas.name: Expected value
formulas.note: The long-run average outcome.

shortcuts.name: At least one = 1 − none
shortcuts.rule: Work out the probability of no successes and subtract it from 1.
shortcuts.example: At least one head in 3 coins: 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. At least one six in two dice throws: 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

shortcuts.name: Two-dice sum count
shortcuts.rule: The number of ways to roll a sum s (from 2 to 12) is 6 − |s − 7|.
shortcuts.example: Sum 9: 6 − 2 = 4 ways, so P = 4/36 = 1/9. Sum 7: 6 ways, P = 1/6.

shortcuts.name: Chain the fractions without replacement
shortcuts.rule: Multiply, reducing the top and bottom by 1 at each step.
shortcuts.example: 5 red and 3 blue balls, two red drawn: 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

shortcuts.name: Card overlap
shortcuts.rule: For 'A or B' with cards, add the counts and subtract the overlap before dividing by 52.

shortcuts.name: Odds to probability
shortcuts.rule: Odds of a : b in favour give P = a/(a + b).
shortcuts.example: Odds of 3 : 5 in favour give P = 3/8, and the probability against is 5/8.

shortcuts.name: Binomial mean and variance at sight
shortcuts.rule: Mean = np and variance = np(1 − p).
shortcuts.example: 20 trials with p = 0.3: mean 6, variance 20 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 4.2.

traps: Treating mutually exclusive as the same as independent.
Adding probabilities for 'A and B' when you should multiply, or multiplying for 'A or B' when you should add.
Forgetting to reduce the denominator when drawing without replacement.
Double-counting the overlap in 'or' questions.
Counting (2, 5) and (5, 2) as one outcome when listing the two-dice sample space.
nsmqTips: For 'at least' and 'not all' questions, go straight to the complement.
Simplify the fraction before you speak. Quizmasters usually accept equivalent fractions, but a simplified answer is clearer.
Learn the deck counts (aces 4, face cards 12, red 26) and the two-dice table so you never have to list outcomes.

topics.summary: This topic is about systematic counting: arrangements where order matters (permutations) and selections where it does not (combinations), with restrictions, repeated items and circular layouts. NSMQ asks counting riddles that are quick with the right model and slow without it.
keyIdeas: Multiplication principle: if a task has stages with m and n choices, there are m × n ways in total.
Use a permutation when order matters (arrangements, rankings, codes) and a combination when it does not (committees, hands, selections).
0! = 1, and ⁿP₀ = ⁿC₀ = 1.
ⁿPᵣ = r! × ⁿCᵣ.
Items that must be together: treat them as one block, then multiply by the internal arrangements.
'Not together' = total − together.
For 'at least' selections, use the complement or add the separate cases.

formulas.name: Factorial
formulas.note: The number of arrangements of n distinct objects in a line.

formulas.name: Permutations
formulas.note: Ordered arrangements of r objects taken from n.

formulas.name: Combinations
formulas.note: Unordered selections of r objects from n.

formulas.name: Symmetry
formulas.note: Choosing r to include is the same as choosing n − r to leave out.

formulas.name: Pascal's rule
formulas.note: Builds Pascal's triangle.

formulas.name: Repeated objects
formulas.note: p, q, r, … are the counts of identical items.

formulas.name: Circular arrangements
formulas.formula: (n − 1)!; if clockwise and anticlockwise count as the same (necklace), (n − 1)!/2
formulas.note: Fix one person to remove rotations.

formulas.name: With repetition
formulas.note: r positions, each filled from n choices, e.g. PIN codes.

formulas.name: Subsets
formulas.formula: Number of subsets = 2ⁿ, ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + … + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ
formulas.note: Non-empty subsets: 2ⁿ − 1.

formulas.name: Binomial general term
formulas.formula: T₍ᵣ₊₁₎ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ in (a + b)ⁿ
formulas.note: There are n + 1 terms.

formulas.name: Geometry counts
formulas.formula: Lines through n points (no three collinear) = ⁿC₂, triangles = ⁿC₃, diagonals of an n-gon = ⁿC₂ − n
formulas.note: Handshakes among n people = ⁿC₂.

shortcuts.name: Use symmetry to shrink r
shortcuts.rule: Compute ⁿCᵣ with whichever of r and n − r is smaller.
shortcuts.example: ¹⁰C₈ = ¹⁰C₂ = 10 × 9/2 = 45. ¹²C₁₀ = ¹²C₂ = 66.

shortcuts.name: Handshake count
shortcuts.example: 12 people each shaking hands once: 12 × 11/2 = 66 handshakes.

shortcuts.name: Divide for repeats
shortcuts.rule: Divide n! by the factorial of each repeated letter's count.
shortcuts.example: LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice: 5!/(2! 2!) = 120/4 = 30.

shortcuts.name: Block then subtract
shortcuts.rule: Together = (n − k + 1)! × k!. Not together = n! − together.
shortcuts.example: 5 people, 2 of whom must sit together: 4! × 2! = 48. Not together: 120 − 48 = 72.

shortcuts.name: At least one by complement
shortcuts.rule: Total selections minus selections with none of the required type.
shortcuts.example: Choosing 3 from 6 men and 4 women with at least one woman: ¹⁰C₃ − ⁶C₃ = 120 − 20 = 100.

shortcuts.name: Round table
shortcuts.rule: Fix one seat, then arrange the remaining n − 1 people.
shortcuts.example: 6 people round a table: 5! = 120. 6 different beads on a necklace: 120/2 = 60.

traps: Using a permutation for a committee, where order does not matter.
Forgetting to multiply by the internal arrangements of a block.
Using n! instead of (n − 1)! for circular arrangements.
Treating identical objects as distinct, which overcounts.
Adding the cases for 'at least one' but missing a case or counting one twice. The complement is safer.
nsmqTips: Ask yourself first: does order matter? That one decision settles most quiz questions.
Memorise small values: 5! = 120, 6! = 720, 7! = 5040, ⁵C₂ = 10, ⁶C₃ = 20, ¹⁰C₃ = 120.
Word clues: 'arrange', 'rank' and 'codes' mean P. 'Select', 'choose', 'team' and 'hand' mean C.

topics.summary: Mechanics applies mathematics to motion and forces. It covers the equations of motion for uniform acceleration, Newton's laws, friction, projectiles, moments, and equilibrium of forces. NSMQ mechanics problems reward choosing the right equation of motion at once and spotting symmetric or standard results.
keyIdeas: The equations of motion (suvat) only hold for constant acceleration.
Resultant force = mass × acceleration. In equilibrium the resultant force is zero.
Friction opposes the motion, or the tendency to move, and its maximum value is μR.
A projectile's horizontal velocity is constant. Vertically it accelerates at g downwards.
For a body in equilibrium, the forces balance in every direction and the moments about any point balance.
The weight of a uniform body acts at its centre: the midpoint of a uniform beam.
Momentum is conserved in collisions when no external impulse acts.

formulas.name: Equations of uniform acceleration
formulas.formula: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t
formulas.note: u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, s = displacement, t = time.

formulas.name: Newton's second law
formulas.note: F is the resultant force in N, m in kg, a in m/s². g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (10 if the question allows).

formulas.name: Friction
formulas.formula: F ≤ μR; limiting friction F = μR
formulas.note: R is the normal reaction. On the point of sliding down a rough slope, tan θ = μ.

formulas.name: Inclined plane components
formulas.formula: Along the slope mg sin θ; perpendicular to it mg cos θ
formulas.note: On a smooth slope the acceleration is g sin θ.

formulas.name: Momentum and impulse
formulas.formula: p = mv; impulse J = FΔt = mv − mu
formulas.note: Conservation: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

formulas.name: Projectile results
formulas.formula: Time of flight T = 2u sin θ/g; maximum height H = u² sin²θ/(2g); range R = u² sin 2θ/g
formulas.note: Launched from level ground at angle θ to the horizontal.

formulas.name: Work, energy, power
formulas.formula: W = Fs cos θ; KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; P = Fv
formulas.note: Units: joules (J) and watts (W).

formulas.name: Resultant of two forces
formulas.note: θ is the angle between the forces.

formulas.name: Lami's theorem
formulas.formula: P/sin α = Q/sin β = R/sin γ
formulas.note: For three forces in equilibrium. Each angle is the one opposite its force, i.e. between the other two forces.

formulas.name: Moments
formulas.formula: Moment = F × perpendicular distance; in equilibrium Σ clockwise = Σ anticlockwise
formulas.note: Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts to remove it.

formulas.name: Connected particles (Atwood machine)
formulas.note: Light string over a smooth pulley, m₁ > m₂.

shortcuts.name: Maximum range at 45°
shortcuts.rule: The maximum range is u²/g. Complementary angles (θ and 90° − θ) give the same range.
shortcuts.example: u = 20 m/s, g = 10 m/s²: maximum range = 400/10 = 40 m. Launches at 30° and 60° land at the same spot.

shortcuts.name: Odd-number rule for free fall
shortcuts.rule: From rest, the distances covered in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7. With g = 10, the distance fallen is s = 5t².
shortcuts.example: Distance in the 3rd second = 5 × 5 = 25 m. Check: s(3) − s(2) = 45 − 20 = 25 m.

shortcuts.name: Stopping distance
shortcuts.rule: With v = 0: s = u²/(2a), where a is the size of the deceleration.
shortcuts.example: u = 20 m/s braking at 4 m/s²: s = 400/8 = 50 m. Doubling the speed makes the stopping distance 4 times as long.

shortcuts.name: Two equal forces
shortcuts.rule: Two forces of size F at angle θ have resultant 2F cos(θ/2), along the bisector.
shortcuts.example: Two 10 N forces at 120°: R = 2 × 10 × cos 60° = 10 N. At 60°: R = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 N.

shortcuts.name: Atwood in one line
shortcuts.rule: a = (difference in masses / total mass) × g. T = 2 × product / sum × g.

shortcuts.name: Split a beam load by distance
shortcuts.rule: A point load W on a beam supported at both ends goes to each support in proportion to its distance from the other support. A uniform beam's own weight splits equally.
shortcuts.example: A 6 m uniform beam of weight 120 N carries a 60 N load 2 m from A. The load gives 40 N at A and 20 N at B; the weight gives 60 N to each. So R_A = 100 N and R_B = 80 N, which sum to 180 N.

traps: Mixing up mass (kg) and weight (N). Weight = mg.
Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6, e.g. 72 km/h = 20 m/s.
Swapping sin and cos when resolving on an incline. The component along the slope is mg sin θ.
Using suvat when the acceleration is not constant, e.g. a = 3t. Use calculus instead.
Getting the sign of g wrong: take one direction as positive and stay with it.
nsmqTips: Write down the three known suvat quantities and the one you want. That picks the equation immediately.
Check whether the question says g = 9.8 or g = 10. Answers are often designed to come out exactly with one of them.
In statics, take moments about the point that removes the most unknowns. Often one line gives the answer.
